blocks.x: This is Paul Crawford.
And this is Richard Allen. Manny J. Mello. We're recording this afternoon of August the 3rd, 1959 at 1025 Betholome Street. So we've got your name on there. You call yourself Manny?
Manny J. Mello. That's what they always did call me. But Manuel is your father. Manuel is your father.
And the first thing we usually like to ask people is the date and place of their birth.
Right here in the Walls, two blocks away from here, 1887. On Betholome? On Betholome in Ibogunny. And the exact date of your birth? June the 4th.
On what year? 1887. 1887. Next. And did any of your family play music in your father's generation? None of them. Played a harmonica.

Your father? No. Just around the house. He never played. Not professional, amateur, semi-professional. He just played. Now they used to play harmonica. That is home for the kids, you know? Next. And your grandfather? None. Nobody. Mm-hmm. Nobody back in that generation? Not nobody in the first generation.
Do you remember any of the tunes your father played on the harmonica?

Oh, yeah. All them old tunes. Swanee River. And I only just wanted to know. Widow done. Six Little Angels. Boy, we're going back now. We're going back now. We used to play that Long Sonata. Oh, yeah? Yeah, Long Sonata used to, because you see, he knew it. And I knew it. And when we played, we had with Jack Lane, Jack Lane to make all kind of four faces. Man, he'd be making faces a day, you know, and Mark McCurt sitting on the side of me. He'd be laughing or just Long Sonata, guitar and the string bass player that kept the music, kept the melody out. We used to play all that old-time stuff. And it used to go. It used to go. This stuff that they play now, what they call jazz, that's as far away from jazz as the moon is from the city of New Orleans. I'm going to tell you what I know. Next, go ahead. Question.
How many brothers did you have? Three. Did they all play music?

Yeah. They all played trombos, string bass, guitar, mandolin. And my second, the fellow under me used to play guitar, only. That was Henry. And my younger brother, he played with Pangelline for a while. He played trap drums.

And what's his name? Sanford. Sanford. They call him Sam? Sam. Sam. And what's the difference in ages there? Oh, I'll be 73 pretty soon. And how old would Leonce be if he were alive? Leonce would be about 68. So you're the oldest. I'm the oldest. And Sanford is the youngest. Youngest. And he's how much younger than you?
Oh, plenty younger. He was born, I think that was in 1903. Mm-hmm. 1903 was born. He was born the year that my daddy died.
And, uh, Henry? Henry was two years younger than I was.
Are the other two still living? Henry and Sam? No. Sam is living, but Henry and Leonce are both dead. Henry died about two years after Leonce.
Well, to get into Leonce's life a little, did he study music?

Yeah, with his ears. With his ears. I'll tell you what, not that he was my brother like I told Crawford. Not that he was my brother. But whatever the heck he put his hands on and he wanted to play, he played. And it didn't matter what he played, he used to go around the nigger bands and listen to the execution. Oh, he'd come home and play it. If he went to the niggers and heard one piece of music, he'd come home and play it. That's just how good a head he had. He could have gone on with Ted Lewis. Ted Lewis wanted he and I both. Leonce says that the only time they're gonna put a frock on him is when he's dead. He wouldn't use no white suit. And he positively wouldn't use no tuxedo. He would not. Uh-uh, Leonce is a queer sort of a doctor. But as queer as he was in music, you couldn't beat him. As good as he was, you couldn't beat him in music. Like I told Crawford, like I tell anybody else. You wanna see how good a musician is? Put him in a funeral and he's gonna play on a beat. Then you'll find out what kind of musician he is. But Leonce just had the knack. He had the head and he had the know-how. That's what you could call it, the know-how. Boy, he could play. He could play and he had a lip like that, that table, hard like that, like me. Now you've seen my trumpet. That trumpet ain't been used since Leonce died. Whenever I'm gonna play a trumpet, Jabba, Google, make a fire, eat it for my brother-law from the other fella down below. I don't know. I never touched that horn. Leonce and I played the last job with that horn. We played at a reception. That was about three years before he died. And just as the horn you see there, that's the way the horn's been set. Because the piano was in international pitch, high pitch. So naturally, you had to put on a high-pitched slide. So we put the high-pitched slide on and as you see that horn then, now, that's the way it was done. He was a good musician. And every time I play music, I always feel it. I got him on the side of me, but the trumpet ain't there. You come back behind you, ain't there at all. So I go out, but I feel worse when I go play music. I don't see if I'm playing around with a whole lot of noise and stuff. That's different. But to go play a real job, boy, that right-handed got him lost. I mean I'm lost. So I miss Leonce. And like I tell you, my horn been in that same position from the day Leonce. So the day we quit playing music, he quit playing. And I ain't touched on him since. Well, when did he die? He died five years ago. And Henry died two years later. I'll tell you, it's pitiful when you know fellas like that, anyhow, you catch a whole lot of fellas that thinks they're musicians. But I'll say this for Leonce, and I'll say it for Leonce again. Leonce never changed the slide on his trumpet. It didn't matter what key you played in. You could play in sharps or flats or any other key. He played. And he had it. But a lot of these fellas in the old days, when you're playing all right, what you're going to play, we're going to play flats. All right, wait, I'm going to put a flat-sized high-pitched slide on it. Now, if you want to play in sharps, he might make, he can play one or two keys in sharps, but he can't play the piece through. He can vamp on it. When you want to play in sharps, you got to wait until he took that phrase and slide out the end of his horn and put another one in. Bring his, lower the pitch on the horn. Not allowance, allowance to put a hang with color. What kind of frasslin' key you played in, he played. I don't care what it was. So, he was a good musician. Now, you take a lot of these niggas that die, and that's what binds me up. The Souchon Brigade, they, I'm not knocking now, but when the niggas died, everybody had to attend the niggas funerals. And when the white fellas died, it was as good or better than the niggas, they couldn't even, even if they wasn't half as good as the niggas. Nobody never showed up. Nobody never showed up. They didn't worry about that. I was just another musician. That's all. Papa Celestine, when Papa Celestine died, the whole frasin' jazz outfit had a possession behind him. When quite a few of the old times, Humpback Gallaty, he was one of the old-time musicians. Leonce was another one. Martin Kurch was another one. Gelo Nunes was another one. Quite a few of the old times, it was real musicians. Nobody had just died and got better than that was all. So, that's the only thing that I don't approve of.
Well, that generation is forgotten today, pretty much. I know.

I know, but today, the generation and the musicians that they have now will never, and you can take that from me as an authority, will never play the music we used to play in our days. For the simple reason is that they didn't, they gave you a program. All right, you play according to the program. Now, that program maybe might have contained 12, 14, or 16 different type dances. Mazzucca, lances, shatters, waltzes, minuets, varieties. That was all on the program, and you played just the way the program was. Show me if any of these fellas is Humpback. And you take in the old days when you got a, you got a, a dance, and you played at a ball, and you see these people dancing. Why? Why? It was a, a, a, something nice to look at. I had a friend of mine who was coming, Pansylane and I, Hookland better known as, who was coming from a layup one night, not a layup, but we went to a meet, and they had a dance on St. Croix and Ann and Roy. So, we came through there, and who was camped there, but Redhill, Lieutenant Redhill, and Louie Kenricks, police. And I says to Louie, I said, what you doing here? Well, he says, I'm learning how to dance. Redhill says, you don't have to know how to dance to dance, that dance. He says, all you got to do is get up and shake your tail, that's all. You're dancing. But which is the truth. Which is the truth. Now, you don't see them dance, you never seen them dance except after 12 o'clock, in places that was known, like the Perfect Union Hall, and back at the Unexpected, back at the Main Street, and the Tonti. Not much at the Tonti, but the Perfect Union on Rampart Street, which has Point Down, and the Unexpected back at the Main Street. You've seen some of that carrying on after 12 o'clock. That's when the rough gang got in. But you don't see, you never seen that in the regular dance. Go to look at the regular dance now and see what you can see. Just take a look at the regular dance now and see what you can see. It's a disgrace. And what I know, I know it to be a positive fact that the old days, these modern times will never revoit back to the old days, that they won't. But the dances will never be the same. Never will be the same. In the old days, you had good dances. And when you danced, and you played a waltz and you seen them dance a waltz, that was something nice to look at. Especially when they had a prize waltz and they chalked their heels. You never heard of that, did you? No. They had about eight or ten fellas on the floor, you know, and they'd be watching you in the prize court. They had good prizes. You put your foot down, find out what happens. You're marks there, you're gone. You're out. You had to dance on your toes all the time. But now, now it's a flat foot dance like the knees used to dance in the old days. So, that's the way the things are running now. Of course, I'm not condemning. Or am I not? I don't want it to be misconstrued that I'm knocking at the present age, or anything else. I'm not. But we just comparing the times, the old times and now. There's nothing more nicer to see than a dance. You go to a dancer that had real dances in. But now, what do you see? Oh, valley hood, wreck them up, bust up, leave one fella, blow his brains out one way and the other fella on the drum beat, and his brains out, what happens? Oh, that's beautiful music. You can't tell what they're playing. You can't. In my band, when I always tried to lead, if I led, let Martin Kurch do the dirty work of Yellow Nunes. If Martin Kurch led, he let me do the dirty work on the drum beat. And we had certain parts there that was just nice work, nice execution for the drum beat. But now what? One fella's trying to go above the staff. It's usurpation of music. That's what it is. You take orchestras from the violin on down. You take the violin, the clarinet, the cornet, the trumbo. You never had saxophone, see? But you never did hear the cornet try to outdo the clarinet. And you never heard the clarinet try to outdo the fiddle. Boy, he'd get out of some position on the fiddle and he'd make you sick. Now, did you ever hear of a mute for a fiddle? I have. You have? Sure. Shove it on a bridge? Yeah. Boy, that's fine, yeah. I played with them fellas. I played with one or two fellas that really could use a mute. And you could play that. They don't absorb the signs in music. Ain't no such thing as canister. It's double 40. Double 40 all the way through. They start off 40 and they end up on double 40. Come right back to double 40. They hit adult single-sided going on right back. No matter if they got one P on the staff or two Ps, they disregard that. See, they're looking at the two Fs. So, we used to... We... I'll say this and I'll say it again. Popeye Lane's living, he'll tell you. We used to play that soft, but you can hear their feet on the floor. You hear that now? Not unless they put sand on their shoes. That's out. I listen to quite a few bands and I hear quite a few fellas say, Oh, I can lay in bed. Music loves me to sleep. Not me. I listen for the rotten notes they make. That's what I do. I listen for the rotten notes. Long before I was married there, we used to have the Nemo Club on Congress in Burgundy. We used to have dances there for the regular anyhow twice a week. We played that quite a few times. And we'd come in maybe from playing our job and they'd have one or two badges to come there. Nigger in there and somebody else. Boy, that was the smell of the band. And Leon said, Leon said, Leon said, Leon said, Leon on that side and I'd be laying on this side in the other room. And I said, Whoa, whoa. Said, you smell that? Rotten notes. Of course, people didn't know it. But that was my trouble. I can lay in this bed right now and hear a band playing. And I don't, uh, I would sleep. I couldn't sleep. Because I wait for the next mother to make a rotten note. A rotten stop or rotten something else. I'll tell you what I do. I like music. I can sit down and talk music all day, all night, and all day. I like music. But I don't like music like they play it now. Here's another thing. You can look for this. Lawrence Welk has a dissension in his band. When he put a half a million more strings in there, and he's got one or two others, that's instead of having in the trumpet section two solos and two poets, you've got them all playing solo. Which is wrong. Anyhow, in a band of each size. He's got a couple of these men quit. But, uh, I told my wife that Saturday a week ago. I says, you know something? She says, what? I said, Lawrence Welk's got a dissension in his band. And I'm the boy who can see it. I'm the boy who can see it. Of course, after you play music as long as I play it, you know when the dissension's starting and when it's not. You can see it. Especially when you get four trumpets working together and then one fella try to outgrow the other and make the most noise and every other present thing. Well, I have one. You want to smoke? Go ahead and hug yourself.
Yeah, I'm gonna get a cigarette. Uh, I was wondering something. How did you get your start in music?
Did you hear any other music than your father playing the harmonica?
Oh, yes.

I heard Brad Stecker, the oldest trumpet player in the city right now. He was, uh, he used to play with, uh, I used to do a little reporting for the International Jazz. That's a year, four years back. And, uh, they used to rehearse once a week on a Wednesday night. On. With a good Betholome in there. Dolphine. And I used to go there. Well, my daddy was a pretty good friend of Shanks. And, uh, I used to go over there and listen to him. Now, I'll say this for Bat Steckler. He could do what I couldn't do. Bat Steckler could take a horn and put a horn in C, in sharps. And play in flats. Or he could put a horn in flats and play in sharps. That's what he could do. That same Bat Steckler you wanted to see. Do you mean by changing the slides? No, he'd never change the flats and things. He never had no slides. And he only had, he used to have two crooks. He had an A crook and a B crook. Little bit of crooks. But one of the B was about that B flat. And the A was about that long. But when he put the A on, it threw his horn in the sharps. He was a C then. Well, he never did do that. If he had that C crook on, well, he just up it on. That's all in play. And he didn't do that. And he didn't do that. So, I tell him that many times. I said Bat got a dog and I said you can do something that I couldn't do. And I tried it time and again. He said, all right, try and put your horn in B flat. And then, try to play in C or in D or in G or you're gonna fight. So, oh, he says, you used to get the tone out of the horn. Yeah, I said, but I couldn't get the difference. I said, no, they had three valves to work. I said, how'd you do it? Well, he said, we did it. I know he did because Johnny Gormason, Johnny Shank used to play practically all in C. But, sometime, he'd get a piece of playing F on B flat. But, I never had changed no crook. No, no, uh-uh. No. And I've seen that. I can still see the four of them sitting there. And that's over 60 years ago.
What were their names? Sheik was one of them?

Yeah. Albert Six was the bass player. They used to call them Engelbats Sinks. Johnny Boimason, Weinmanson, he was a guitar player. Johnny Shank was a fiddle player. And Batstucker was a cornet player. Well, that's the first string band that I know of that had a blowing instrument in it. All the rest of them had a bass violin guitar man and a bass violin guitar three piece band, you know? So, he was the first one that played with a blowing horn in it. Bat was good. Bat used to be a case. Brick Lane today go play music at night. That was a combination, wasn't it? Mm-hmm. I go back up his house plenty. But right now, I've been laid up. I got an inflamed sciatic noise, man, and my messed up. I can't navigate the way I want. I'd like to go see Bat because Bat used to both played in the swamp. Plenty, plenty, plenty. And I go back there, Bat is music from the time we start until the time we finish. I like Bat Stuckler. But he is really the last of the old times. Next to him comes me. Did he play what you call a jazz cornet? He played ragtime. Ragtime. Ragtime was a little bit, the tempo was a little bit increased. That's the jazz. And after the jazz came out, why? We used to play jazz because the niggas used to play jazz. At that time, they only had two bands, two dance bands. That was the Imperial and Superior. And the Onward and Excelsior that I can remember of was the marching bands for feudals and stuff. The Imperial and Superior were the two bands. Now, I'm going back to about 1905, 1906, something like that. Maybe a little bit, say, 1904. 1904, five, and six. And all these other fellas started taking up music and the bands split up. And that's the way it was. But, uh, they always go back there and steal the niggas music and come there and play it on the man. Play it about twice. We go play it at a dance. We used to have, between Lawrence and I, I tell you, I lost my right arm when he died. But Scott and Dogger, he had this, and he had this.
He had which, I couldn't see, he had that head to here? I couldn't see what you were pointing to.

No, his head, he had the brains and he had the ear. I see. He had the head, the brains, and the ear. What did you say he first started playing? Manning. And then he switched to... To guitar. And then he played what? Bass, string bass. And then? Trombone. Sliphorn. Sliphorn.
Mm-hmm.

And, uh, he was good. I'm going to tell you what I know. Not that he's my brother, was my brother, but I'll hold his end up any time, because you can take a few fellas that knew Lawrence, and they'll tell you what kind of trombone player he was. He was a trombone player. I played with some good trombone players. I played with Eddie Benton, I played with Eddie Riley. I played with, uh, Humpback Gallaty. Now, Bill Gallaty wasn't much of a slide man, but he was a pretty good tenor trombone player. That's Val? Val. Tenor. Val. Val. Val. Val. Val. Val. Val. Val. Val. Val. He's the first one, Leonce is the first one that I can remember of. He played bass one night and he filled in on for a fella, I don't know who got sick. He filled in for a fella and I see him with a drumstick in his pocket. He said, what did he play drums too? He said, no, I'm going to pick a bass. I'm going to pick a bass with a drumstick. He said, you don't think that I'm going to bust up all my fingers, he says, picking on strings. And we used to tune up B-Natural. We used to tune up on high pitch, not no low pitch, high pitch. When you start picking on a string bass, I mean make it slap. I don't mean boom, boom, boom like they're picking out and just pick on the strings like that. I mean make it slap and you got some way. No, it's just a bit of a picnic sometimes. Got it all there. Alright, next. Did you have any teachers yourself? Me? Mm-hmm. Well, across college, for the riding, have you ever caught your foot down your foot like you do now? You don't do that music. You don't do that music. So you could read now. What was his name? Father what? Father Rutter. Writer they called him, but he's a R-E-U-T-H-E-R. He was enjoyment. He was enjoyment.
You know, I noticed you mentioned a lot of Germans with Steckler by name that they sound like... It was all Germans.

It was all Germans. Baptiste is the only Frenchman. His name is Jean-Baptiste Steckler. And I used to laugh, my daughter. He was a case. He still is a case. Yeah, I learned down at Holy Cross College. And when I started playing with what we call a GDNC band, that is four pieces or five pieces, they could play and I couldn't because I could read and they could and I couldn't fake. They could fake what I couldn't read. Boy, was a dag-gun this time trying to get next to that, but it didn't take long. It didn't take long. It didn't take long at all. We run through a piece once or twice. We stole a nigga Zalipo's music out at the... That picture I showed you? The circus? We stole Zalipo's music. I didn't steal it, but Leon is the one who lifted it. He didn't lift it, he borrowed it. Next morning we run over it once or twice. The Dine Rag and the Honky Tonky Monkey Rag. Let's see what else. They had another one they used to have there too. So long I forgot. But we run over that thing, come out that night, say, alright Zalipo. Zalipo is the nigga comedian. He was good. And this nigga's go. Of course I'm not, I don't praise. Colored brothers. Strictly all white. So, I said, alright Zalipo, we're gonna play you a piece. We're gonna play professor and we're gonna play the Dine Rag. I said, we're gonna play the Dine Rag. I said, you don't know the Dine Rag. And we used to play all 6-8 stuff out there. That was all 6-8 movement. That wasn't no slow stuff. That was 6-8 movement. I played the Dine Rag and the Honky Tonky Mama Rag and the Good Time Mama Rag. That's what it was. Zalipo, they had big eyes already, but his eyes got that big. He said, how come you fellas ever played that? He didn't know that the buyer is from the nigga piano player. I used to laugh. I used to kick myself. But it ain't no more like that. It ain't no more like that. But when you play now, you play your regular hand organ. That's what you all hand organ. They play sets. So many pieces to a set. And after that set, when you get about 10 minutes to go down and get a drink, and you come back, you play six or seven more sets. Boy, you're going like a pornograph. If that was me, I'd get one of them dancers. Uh-uh. I'd bring a radio with me. I'd say, all right, we're gonna play by the radio. Because they work you to death. A few places that we play, you know, all dead well. We don't play that kind of music. We play a couple of pieces, and then we go back and see if we got something to drink back there. Of course, I can drink on account of that frazzled stomach of mine. My stomach was getting bad all the way through. And usually the last time, I couldn't drink. I couldn't even drink water. And when I did drink water, I had a squeeze of half a lemon in it. My stomach really went acid. So, uh, we don't play that kind of music like I play now. Uh-uh. No. All right, Mr. Allen, what next?
Which was your very first job playing music professionally? Professionally?

We played for the Green Roof Social Club, Marais and Bethania. William Schenk was there. He was the proprietor of the saloon and the Green Roof, too. That was the first job I ever played. With a magnificent sum of $2, four hours. That wasn't bad for those days. No, it was pretty good. Next.
Whose band was it?

Weimanson's band. That's the first band I ever started out to get real, get real tamed up, you can say. Because I could play, go out and play a professional job that I could. But I didn't want that so much. But I wanted to get a sound to make a whole lot of noise. I learned how to make noise. I learned how to make noise. I believe they. And what year was that? It was in 1903. around that time? Well, they, let's see.
They did have, Steckler, Steckler's band went out of, uh, they, they, they, they, they,

they disbanded. And, and, and, and the, uh, Spanish-American war why one or two of the fellow signed up and went to the army and the band, why just disbanded and they was never reorganized. So let's see, they had another band. I believe that was O'Ramus' band. That was three pieces. Guitar, bass, and violin.

The You're talking about Ramis' band? Or Amis. Or Amis. That's the only other string band that I knew of at that particular time that was playing. And it's going around a three-piece job, not a whole lot of... Just, they never played a whole lot of big music. They played three pieces bass, violin, guitar. And what would they play like? Would they play by music? No, no, by hand.

So everybody with the exception of Schilling and Philly Marsloff, but Marsloff wasn't in the brass band. Schilling took up ten of trombone. We got Eddie Riley, we got the two Dykemans, we got Roy Bridges, playing trap drums with us then. We formed a brass band and the brass band stuck, oh I guess in about 1909. The Fisher still had his band, he had Richie Brunus leading it, but he didn't go too far with it. What did Marsloff play? Marsloff's guitar. Paper hang about that, guitar play about that. And the Dyke ones, what are they?

T. Notchie Beg, uh, Lance composed that piece, and that was a real, real nigger piece. I mean, you talk about it as close to being colored. Manny Perez, he's dead in not quite a while, and he told Lance, he says, that was, he says, the most best nigger piece that I ever did here. He says, that really was a nigger piece. I tell you. And I said, oh, he just composed. Lance was pretty good. He was good. I still say, well, we used to have a three piece band, cornet, guitar, and bass. The brother band. And that was everything. We'd go play for some of these old times, you know, they wanted, they wanted all this kind of, old kind of music. Of course, these young folks now, they don't look for that kind of music no more. But you can tell old people, they wanted walk, waltzes, mazookas, they wanted to shout us, and then around 11 o'clock that night, the long come old man there, he said, all right, he says, get yourself ready, he says, get yourself a sandwich and a beer, he says, because we're gonna put the lances on. And that was five parts. And that was something to play, cornet, guitar, and bass. We played it. We could go to town on that stuff. When did the blues come in? Well, the blues came in around, around 19, say around 1906. Real blues came in. W.C. Handy composed the St. Louis blues. I ain't heard one of them ever play the St. Louis blues right yet. Now the fellas that composed High Society, they said Buddy Bowles composed that. That's the Bologna, Alphonse Pico composed that piece. And, uh, the blues came in around 1906. We used to, uh, we used to play the blues, but not them kind of blues. But they're all, practically all the blues that you get now is always, it's on the same pattern all the way through. But you take, now you take this Boogie Woogie stuff, you can take it from one who knows. You know what that is? That's the old time color dance. That's when they used to get out there with their feet. Oh, I used to put their feet on board. They used to put it on. I mean put it on. And, uh, that's, that's Boogie Woogie. They call that Boogie Woogie now. But that's the same old tempo, same old method of playing, same rhythm, they used to play it like at L-I-V-A. What's that? L-I-V-A?
Yeah, Ladies Independence Benevolent Association.

Colored that was with a beating heart with a colored folks. They used to have a dance every Saturday night. L-I-V-A had to get all that stuff because L-I-V-A had to have to hit a piece twice or three times before I could play it. But then L-I-V-A had to hit that thing once. Lance, Lance, he'd hit that thing once. Boy, he might make one or two humbugs on it, but he ain't gonna make too many humbugs. He had a quick ear and a good ear. I mean a real good ear. Did you tell me one time that he used to go around to some of the joints where the neighbors were playing? Yeah, yeah, yeah. They taught Lance as a professor. They taught Lance as a professor. Do you remember who he heard around at those places? Well, he used to hear the Imperium and Superior. That was the only two bands that really prayed. Back in the Red Light District, Eddie Souchon, everyone Souchon said that he named the men that they had a Tom Anderson. Tom Anderson's band was composed of a bass, a violin, a guitar, and a vowel trombone, a tenor trombone. That's what Tom Anderson had. And Lance would go around there and listen to all them fellas. They used to call Lance the professor. Alan wanted him to teach his trombone player how to play music. Who is that, Alan? Nigga Allen from Dretton. And we was over the river a couple of times and they'd come over there and they'd be listening, you know, listening to Lance by Trumbo. That's the one there. I was up at the Louis Cresson's some years ago and Manny Perez's wife, he used to be the trumpet player for the Imperial Office, the colored man. And I went to Louis Cresson and says, Mello, he says, you know who this woman is? I says, I do not. He says, that's Manny Perez's wife. And Louis Cresson says to Manny Perez's wife, the other nigga, says, that's Mello, the trumpet player. He says, well, Manny never said much. He only was a good trumpet player. He said, but he sure knew Lyle. He sure knew Lyle. Lyle would go around there, steal all of these music and come back and play it. Oh, it was a case. I just liked to hear Lyle play Frumbo than somebody else. I could just hear the parts that he put in, you know, God told him. And he had the knack of putting them in. He had the knack of putting them in. And he knew when and how and what time. So, we had Jacqueline tell you about this. Played a funeral procession over there. And he said, who you got in the lineup? I said, well, he said, we're going to use the old wire face. There he goes, that was old man Alessandro. And his son, Manuel, used to call him Little Wire Face. He says, we're going to use Alessandro on tuba. He says, we'll use Brock on barbond. He said trombone. I said, Lyle. He looked at me. I said, Lyle. It's all right. So, we had Joe Castro and Joe Castro and Little Wire Face, they're going out to us. With them old, that Little Dago had one of them rotary valves. You ever see them old Dago horns, rotary valves? They got good action to him. He said, all right. We started off, man. We tore them up going to the where the old throw was laid out. and got there, played the piece, played the Nero of my God, when they took them out. And then when when we started off, and we got a half a block away, we started off going to the church. old Jack Lennon. I said, what's the matter? He said, he played it. He pressed me on the bus. Well, Lyle's had the knack. He had the knack to play that kind of music. Lyle's playing the kind of music. He'd play opera. He couldn't read a note. He'd play opera and he couldn't read a note.
Did Lyle's work with many bands that you didn't work with? Well,

he worked with Galatay. He worked with Christian. He worked with Baraka. And he worked with Monjada, Triangle Officer. Which Monjada's in it? Sato. Sam. The clarinet player? I believe it is. And which Christian? Frank Christian played cornet. And Beans Christian, Emil, he played cornet. And who else did the horse play? He lost the horse to somebody else. His main hole after he left us was to play with Frank Christian. We made a swap. I took Charlie and he went over to play. Plus he had some kind of disagreement with Jack Lane. It used to be. It was a pretty good swap when I took Charlie over and he told me that I was going to have two tubas in the band. I told the fellow that told me that and he was supposed to be a good friend of mine and he ain't no friend of mine. I found out to be a double crosser. I says, well, I'd soon have two tubas and two cornets. He says, you know what you're talking about. I said, maybe I don't because Charlie Christian played everything in the bass clap. Charlie couldn't play in treble clef to save his cell or slide from home. He'd play like that on a horn. On that horn he had, man, when he'd get half drunk and him and Jack Lane get all the pickups, drop all the drugs and he'd out on the floor. I never seen Martin Abraham for a long time. Anybody, you ever seen Martin Abraham lately? I haven't seen him lately. Have you, Paul? Just in March. First of March, I guess, was the last time I saw him. Is he playing in town? Just some spots, I think. I think he made, he might have made a record with Raymond, Burke, not too long ago. I'm not sure.
I haven't heard anything from him in a long time.

Boy, he got the swell head. Did he get a swell head? I had Martin Abraham to chink with me when he had one, two pair shoes. He had a pair of white shoes and a pair of black shoes and a pair of white pants and a pair of black pants. And that was all. That was all. He had a wife with about 40 kids. He used to live up in the jungles on Royal Strait. But I had Martin with me a good long time. Martin was a pretty good bass player. But the fellow that learned Martin how to play bass, and he had a good guitar player. When he died, Martin didn't even pay him no mind. Didn't even go see him. That was Alex Pizzita. He used to live out on Moss Street on Boston John. Alex was a good guitar player. When Jacqueline reorganized his band and I took over, we had Alex Pizzita on guitar. The chick was on bass and had Yellen Lunes on clarinet. Oh, he was triped. And Lance played trombone, I played cornet. Jack Lane played trap drums. Now, he had a complete set of drums. He had a single-head snare drum, an orchestra drum, bells, sand block, wood block, triangle, crass, angled, cymbal. I forget what else he had. That was one way organized the Reader Alliance band. And the last job I played with Jack Lane over the river, had to kick the rungs out of a chair to make the drumsticks. He had nothing. Had nothing. He had a snare drum with two batty heads on. Instead of a snare head and a batty head, he had two batty heads on it. That thing would kill you. He used to use the snare side, batty head on the snare side. Then when he'd sit down to play a job, he had to tie the bass drum to the chair so it wouldn't get away from it. The traps. The traps consisted of one bar with a nickel baseball on the end and the shade spring with an additional shade spring on the side in case that didn't let it go. That was the trap. Pedal? Pedal was a homemade pedal. That's what it ended up in. My mom would tell you about it. Martin Abraham, how long Jack laying the money to buy Martin Abraham that tuba out of here? How long did the money? We made good money on the parades. And after that, we'll go to Benny Maas and get the money from Benny Maas for the parades. Of course, Benny Maas used to run the parades. Yeah, charge the parades. So he'd issue the checks. He'd issue the checks. Jack Lynn would get about $40. I got a little red book in there to tell you how much Jack Lynn used to order. Look at that parade. After he played that parade, it was just too bad. He got about $40. I bought a pound out. The parade just to run up my money. Unless we used to split the liter price between him and I. So there it was. As far as music, I like music. I like it and I love it. But I always miss that fellow on the side of me. I tell you, when you get used to playing with somebody, Eddie Benton's a good trombone player. You ever hear of Eddie Benton? Eddie Benton? He's working as a revamp and repairman and wise. You can go up there and see him any time you want. Just walk up. Don't pay nobody no mind. Just walk up. He's in a little hole in the corner like that. If you want to go up and see him, just tell him I said about that. He played trombone with the Sonora Auguste with Joe Huston and I. Joe Huston, Leonis, Sue Sue Ramis, no clarinet, Brad Stevens on the rocks. What did Joe Huston play? He was playing string bass. He was playing string bass. He was playing string bass. There's one thing I said about Huston. Of course, Huston wasn't up to the pieces. It didn't matter what key you put him in, he played. When you put a fella in three flats ball in the fiddle, he's looking for it. Not him. He had it. He was a good musician. Although he didn't read, but he was a good musician right on. That musicians go. All right, Captain, what you got else on your mind?
I'd like to know the names of some of the places where you used to play. Well, I played

in every hall this side of the river from Mac Main's funeral call on Napoleon Avenue, our fellow's hall. I played the Athenaeum, played Stoll's hall, I played the Portuguese hall, I played Tolman's hall, I played back of Beatus, I played at the other hall on Almonster, I think in Oikwa, they had a hall there. The Bowie, I think they called themselves. And I played the Pink's, I played Kambasa's hall, I played the St. Maurice hall, I played the Crescent City Carnival Club on this side of the river. On the other side of the river, everything that had a dance floor in, Crescent Park, Lee Hall, Arlington's Hall, Owls Hall, Suburban Park, Suburban Park Racetrack, Belleville Park, and Elmire Pleasure Ground, and I played down what they used to call the canal. They had it all down there. There. Not counting, not counting the parties and houses went out in the reception.
Did they have special picnic grounds? Oh, yeah.

Yeah. I played Southern Park, that was a special picnic. It used to be the Magnolia Guard because once they used to call it, that was out on by St. John. I played the stocks at City Park. I played every hall on this side of the river, every hall on that side of the river. Every lawn party on, every lot that ever had a lawn party on this side of the river was playing.
What about out of town? Did you get out of town? Oh, yeah.

I went to Slidell, Biloxi, Bay St. Louis, uh, uh, what's the name of the other place? Slidell, and they had another place over there. We played Madisonville, Mandeville. We played pretty well. Oh, it was a pain in the neck, them out of town jobs. A couple of bad pain in the neck because after you got through playing, you had to sit in the dark and fight mosquitoes until it was time for the train to come.
When did Tom Brown come on the scene?

I played a Tom Brown's band when, uh, I can name you the lineup of that band. They had Joe Cazard, the voice vocalist in any band. Detective Cazard, he died. Sometimes, a couple of years ago. I played a guitar. Had Joe Cazard on bass, Jules Cazard on, uh, on guitar. Had Yellow Nunes on clarinet. I played cornet. Gumjaw Brown played, uh, played trombone. And they had Rye Stevens on drums. Played, uh, Seven Magazine, the old majestic call. And Joe was the voice vocalist that any band ever had. How,
what year was that?
Oh, I guess that was around 1905, 1904, something. 1904, 1905. That was a pretty
well-organized band?

That was a pretty good band. All that thing, Gumjaw, got kind of crazy. And, uh, you start to beat up, Ed, you never can hear of a trombone player leading a band. You want to be the leader, you want to be this, and you want to be that, so, I picked up and left him. Yellow left him. Rag Stevens, he left him. He practically lost all these men. You had, he wound up with, uh, the trombone, the guitar, and the bass player. Joe Kazardt was the originator of the police minstrels. Joe could sing. I always used to kid him. The last time I seen Joe Kazardt was when they barred Archbishop Shaw. And he'd give me a big hello. I used to tell Joe, I said, I can croak better than you can sing. Joe's a good singer. He's the first fellow ever sang with a band. The first fellow. What about Johnny Bowman? Johnny Bowman played bass. He didn't sing, he just played bass. He had him, Eddie Edwards on guitar, Gus Miller on clarinet. I played the corner. No trombone. Four pieces. That was long part of the layouts, too. Boy, he'd get out there, he'd be playing at home with one hand, slap the skittles at the other. Gus Miller used to take, and he'd come out there with a great big white handkerchief. You can see him yet. Put it all over his head, all over his neck, and hang it over his ears like this. Oh, boy, that was a layout for me. Skittles. Played that park with the guy out over at the Black Bridge. Played that park. Say, I don't know why I'm wondering how the devil's fellas is going to carry two pints of honey. We can manage. I better tell my wife to see if we can find some paper bags. Boy, you got room in there? Yeah, we can put some in there.
One of them in there, I'm sure. Two of them. We've got plenty of hands, though.

If it's honey, I can carry all the equipment, and he can carry the honey. Uh-uh. No, I don't mean that he gets it all. I know. We better watch the properties heavier than you. He's heavier than you. I hope so. I used to be heavy, but, man, I got it in the back. Then I got high blood pressure, 265. Boy, right then and they put me on a diet. Can't eat this, can't drink that. I had several acidosis. I ain't supposed to drink that. I used to have some which is supposed to be social. All right.
Did they ever use any hymns in any of these jazz tunes? Any who? Hymns. You know, religious tunes. No, no, no. You know, they do that now. You hear them take these spirals. Yeah. Yeah,

they, they, they, they use some of them. And we never did that. We had no occasion, for the simple reason it was, we had a repertoire that we could play all night and never play the same thing over. When you play 32 dances at a ball in six hours, and you don't play no repeats, you ain't, you don't need no hymns. Did Jacqueline ever tell you about the day we put on the German band over the river? No, I didn't. Did you ever hear the Logical Point? Yes, I have heard of that. Did you ever hear it, Parker? No. We went over there to play a parade for the Logical Point in Algiers. So Martin Kirch, Joe Castro, my brother Lance, and myself, Martin says, what you say if we play the German band? So we was waiting for the parade to start, you know. So, all right, we walked about a block away from where the band was congregated, got out on the corner and played German band music, you know. And by the time they had her on and put the peak in the back, let's play German music like sailor hats. You know, Martin Kirch went around with his hat, you know, he was going to start collecting. Don't you know, I believe it again, that fella money? And when the people went to get money, they said, now, we just do it after fun. Well, Papa laying like they had a duck. And he didn't have a duck. That's the kind of fun we used to have. Martin Kirch, he told him, he says, spots, he didn't call them that, he called them something else. He says, if you ever come around with anything like that, he says, there ain't gonna be enough of you left, he says, to feed the fish. Oh, what's the matter with Jewish, he says. Don't put nothing like that off. We was a German band calling it tuba, trombone, clarinet. The German band used to go around at that particular time, see? and we had them down pat. Boy, I can see that, as good as if it happened last night. Boy, it was Papa Lane mad. See, man, he was burnt up. He called Martin everything that he could think of under the sun. He told him he was gonna do him too. Boy, Martin says, you gotta have a little fun, you can't have no fun with you. But Martin had his hat and then he was going around in God on. Everybody was standing out, you know, who was standing at the corner playing German music. He got up with his hat. People were gonna put something in there. They said, no, we're just doing that for fun.
Did you ever rag up

any of those Germans in? Yeah, we played German music. We used to play for the Toine Verand. Toine his heart. That was all German music. Deiz Lene Aries Augustine ! Alley, Harlow, Rosser Schimmel Schmoll, all kind of German pieces. I used to do them doito. They used to have fine liver sausage. And also they had limboiga cheese. They had two kinds of bread. had what they called black bread. And they had French loaf. But when I come in and see the whole stuff packed on the table I get myself a liver sausage and get a knife. And get my bread. And go up on the bandstand. That was on Friday. And that time I could speak jointly. And that was mostly all of the brewmasters and the breweries used to be tagging up in that house. What's good you calling that? I says, yeah. I says, you ain't cutting none of that privy cheese. I says, it'll give me something to eat on my liver. I says, uh-uh. I told him, I says, I told him a gentleman. I says, well, I says, if you care, too, I says, you eat that stuff. I said, you go to Beckhurst. I went to privy. Better known as the toilet. I says, you eat it. I said, you don't know whether you're getting that or you're getting this limbo of your cheese on your hand. And they used to laugh. They used to laugh to beat the band. We played for them a long time, too, until the war. And the war broke it up.
Did they have many piano players in those days? They had a few.

They never had too many of them, though. They had a few of them. But we didn't need no piano. Jacqueline never thought that we could, none did I. I didn't think. In the first place, where we played, we played mostly in the open. And when we played in a place in the hall, so they had pianos. But they were so low that you couldn't tune up with them. You never had enough slide to pull out. And you couldn't transpose enough to put him natural, or put you natural, and him transposed, or him natural, and you transposed. So we did without the piano. Like I tell you, they never even had any recording machines. Never had no, they never recorded no music at all. There was no records made in the city at that particular time. And that's why we didn't get down on plate. But I'm sorry I never had it at that time, because just to show a couple of the good brothers that thought they knew it all and composed pieces that played when they was running around in three corner pants. Go ahead, Crawford. Finish that. Okay. I wanted to ask you, after the war, you continued playing, but were you playing with brass bands or mostly just jazz bands? No, I had my own band. After the First World War. Yeah. I had my own band. What was it called? Mellow's Arrillo. Same as that chord that I showed you. I had Joe Castro on tuba. I had Joe Polizzi on clarinet. I had Bullshank on drums, Emil Bullshank on drums. I played cornet. Pete Dentron played cornet and I also played trombone. Who was going to? Joe Castro told me, and he told us the people over there, but we belonged to the, oh, can't think of the name of that president, club they had over there. But anyhow, he said that he made more money with me in one week than he made with Jacqueline in a month. We was going every night, every night in the week and in the day, Saturday and Sunday in the day. But then it tightened up on me in the tropics. So it was either case of wanting and I couldn't afford to turn $3,500 down for five months' work. So I left Pete Dentron under a band a while, but I don't know, they had a dissension and eventually disintegrated. Made money down there, made money here. Got a hell of a lot better then than I feel now. But they ain't got, I shouldn't feel that bad. If it wasn't for the sciatic and the other one, I'd be all right. But that horn that you've seen, that horn even touched his last, I don't know, I'm not playing. But that's a horn. That, did he play, he played pretty much until, you said a couple, three years before he died? Yeah, just about. And he was playing around here? Yeah, he was playing around here. Who did he play with? George Rispoy, and really I never, I never seen much allowance because I was out of town most. And I never seen much, I know he played with George Rispoy, I don't know. And, if ever I'd get up and play a piece of music in front of any gang, particularly that gang, at that famous jazz club, I'd like to dedicate the number I played to that the good brothers that played with me before I played with us and passed on. That goes for a whole lot of them. I think it's no more, that's a one-sided outfit. They used to send me cards and cards and cards and cards, but there ain't no use of me going up there. I'd only get myself in the jam. So I said, there's more big feeling musicians up there now. Jack Lane will tell you that. Lane told me, he told Benny Mars that one night, he says, you know, he said, as long as I got that thing in the band, he said, I'm a damn, but I'll never get another cornet. He said, one cornet's enough for ten, man. Now how you like that? But I had to look like that table. And I never did guitar, I couldn't guitar. And I love you. You got to love music to play music, and to play music, you got to love music.

segments.title: Opening of the 1959 interview and name
segments.summary: Crawford and Allen identify themselves, give the date and address, and Mello says he is called Manny.

segments.title: Birth in 1887 and father's harmonica
segments.summary: Mello was born in 1887 near the interview house; no relatives were professional musicians, but his father played harmonica tunes like Swanee River.

segments.title: His three brothers and their ages
segments.summary: His brothers Henry, Leonce and Sanford all played instruments; he is the eldest, Sanford born 1903, and Leonce and Henry have died.

segments.title: Brother Leonce's ear, his trumpet and funerals of old musicians
segments.summary: Leonce learned by ear, refused to wear fancy dress, and never changed slides; Mello hasn't touched their trumpet since, and complains that white musicians' funerals draw few attendees.

segments.title: Old-time dances versus modern bands
segments.summary: Mello says today's musicians cannot play the program of waltzes, lancers and mazurkas, and describes prize waltzes, rowdy late dances and 'rotten notes'.

segments.chapter: Early string bands and first jobs
segments.title: Bat Steckler and changing keys on cornet
segments.summary: Asked how he got started, Mello recalls hearing Bat Steckler, who could play in any key by swapping crooks, and rehearsals he attended.

segments.chapter: Early string bands and first jobs
segments.title: The first string band with a horn; ragtime and jazz
segments.summary: The Steckler string band was the first with a blowing instrument; ragtime became jazz, and Imperial and Superior were the dance bands around 1904-06.

segments.chapter: Early string bands and first jobs
segments.title: Leonce's instruments and trombone playing; teachers
segments.summary: Leonce moved from mandolin to guitar, string bass and trombone; Mello praises him and names other trombonists he played with, then mentions Father Reuther at Holy Cross as a teacher.

segments.chapter: Early string bands and first jobs
segments.title: German musicians, learning at Holy Cross, and the Zalipo rags
segments.summary: Mello says the early players were mostly German, describes learning to read at Holy Cross and faking with small bands, and playing borrowed rags for the comedian Zalipo.

segments.chapter: Early string bands and first jobs
segments.title: First professional job at the Green Roof Social Club
segments.summary: His first paid job was $2 for four hours at the Green Roof Social Club with Weimanson's band, around 1903.

segments.chapter: Early string bands and first jobs
segments.title: Steckler's band ends; Ramis's string trio
segments.summary: Steckler's band broke up when members joined the army in the Spanish-American War, leaving Ramis's three-piece string band.

segments.chapter: Early string bands and first jobs
segments.title: Forming a brass band around 1909
segments.summary: Mello and others including Schilling, Eddie Riley and the Dykemans formed a brass band about 1909 while Fisher's band declined.

segments.title: Lancers, the blues around 1906 and boogie woogie
segments.summary: Mello describes three-piece dance jobs and the five-part lancers, dates the blues to about 1906, and says boogie woogie is the old colored dance rhythm.

segments.title: Leonce's quick ear and listening to Black bands
segments.summary: Leonce, called the professor, learned by listening to the Imperial and Superior bands, and played a funeral by ear, even opera, without reading music.

segments.title: Bands Leonce played with; the Christian swap
segments.summary: Leonce also worked with other bands, and Mello recalls a swap involving Charlie Christian and a disagreement with Jack Laine.

segments.title: Martin Abraham, Alex Pizzita and Jack Laine's drums
segments.summary: Mello recalls Martin Abraham, the reorganized Laine band lineup, Laine's homemade drum set, parade pay from Benny Mass, and Eddie Benton and Joe Huston.

segments.chapter: Halls, towns and Tom Brown's band
segments.title: Halls, parks and out-of-town jobs
segments.summary: He lists dance halls, parks and picnic grounds on both sides of the river, and out-of-town jobs in Slidell, Biloxi and Mandeville.

segments.chapter: Halls, towns and Tom Brown's band
segments.title: Tom Brown's band, Joe Cazard and a later quartet
segments.summary: Mello gives the lineup of Tom Brown's band around 1904-05, why he left Gumjaw Brown, and Joe Cazard, plus a later four-piece with Johnny Bowman.

segments.chapter: Halls, towns and Tom Brown's band
segments.title: Honey and Mello's health
segments.summary: Chat about carrying honey and Mello's high blood pressure and diet.

segments.title: No hymns; the German band prank in Algiers
segments.summary: Mello says they played no hymns because of their large repertoire, then tells how he and others played German band music at a parade in Algiers, angering Laine.

segments.title: Playing German music for the brewery crowd
segments.summary: They played German pieces for a German society, where Mello recalls the food, until the war ended it.

segments.title: No pianos or recordings; Mello's own band after World War I
segments.summary: Mello explains why they played without pianos or records, then describes his own post-WWI band with Joe Castro and a lucrative out-of-town job, and Leonce's last years.
